official_sources.finding: GDALChecksumImage computes a 16-bit checksum in the range 0-65535 for a selected raster region.
GDALChecksumImage converts floating-point raster data to 32-bit integer, so decimal portions do not affect that checksum.
GDALChecksumImage returns -1 on error starting with GDAL 3.6, so checksum error state must be distinguished from a valid checksum.
GDALChecksumImage is window-addressed by x/y offset and width/height, so the exact checksum window belongs in replay provenance.
gdal raster info --checksum forces per-band checksum computation and can be used as an independent raster QA signal.
GDAL Python Band.Checksum delegates to GDALChecksumImage, so Python replay inherits the same checksum semantics and limitations.
gdal_translate strict mode fails instead of silently performing information-losing operations such as non-preserving data-type conversion.
gdal_translate can force explicit output types including Float32 and Float64; terminal dtype must therefore be pinned.
gdal_translate may perform subsetting, resampling or rescaling, so a format-conversion step cannot be assumed numerically neutral without an explicit operation manifest.
Changing output type can change representable numeric precision; exact terminal replay must record source and destination dtypes.
The GDAL GeoTIFF driver supports both Float32 and Float64 for reading and writing, allowing storage precision to differ between otherwise similar terrain products.
GTiff DISCARD_LSB explicitly clears least-significant bits and is documented as a lossy compression scheme.
GTiff PREDICTOR=3 is the floating-point predictor for supported floating-point sample sizes, so predictor configuration belongs in file-level provenance.
GeoTIFF block/tile size is configurable and is a storage property; logical terrain-cell identity must not be derived from block layout.
GeoTIFF supports several compression modes whose availability depends on build/driver capabilities; compression configuration must be captured for byte-level replay.
COG PREDICTOR can be set explicitly to STANDARD or FLOATING_POINT, so exact storage creation options can be versioned rather than inferred.
numpy.finfo reports machine limits for a selected floating dtype, making dtype-specific precision an explicit runtime property.
numpy.finfo links floating precision to eps/spacing/nextafter rather than a fixed decimal-place assumption.
numpy.spacing returns the distance between a finite value and the nearest adjacent representable floating value.
NumPy core math defines nextafter as the next representable floating value from x toward y.
NumPy core math defines spacing as the distance from x to the next representable floating value and reports NaN for NaN or infinity.
NumPy floating types include subnormal values below the smallest normal value, so precision checks near zero cannot use smallest_normal as the absolute positive floor.
numpy.nextafter can independently probe the immediate representable neighbour of an extrema value for tie/rounding QA.
For finite x there should be no representable floating value between x and x+spacing(x), enabling ULP-scale audit records.
JSON number grammar does not permit NaN or Infinity.
RFC 8259 permits implementations to impose limits on accepted numeric range and precision.
RFC 8259 notes broad interoperability when implementations expect no more precision or range than IEEE 754 binary64.
JSON Canonicalization Scheme exists to produce invariant representations suitable for repeatable hashing/signing.
JCS uses deterministic property sorting as part of canonical JSON generation.
JCS constrains input to the I-JSON subset before canonicalization.
JCS/I-JSON forbids duplicate JSON object property names.
JCS requires parsed JSON string data to remain unchanged during subsequent serialization.
JCS requires JSON numeric data to be expressible as IEEE 754 double-precision values.
JCS recommends representing numbers requiring higher precision or longer integers as JSON strings.
JCS canonicalization rejects NaN and Infinity rather than serializing them.
JCS defines canonical number serialization through ECMAScript-compatible IEEE 754 serialization rules.
Python json encoding defaults allow NaN and Infinity even though that behavior is not JSON-specification compliant.
Setting allow_nan=False makes Python's JSON encoder reject NaN and Infinity instead of emitting non-standard tokens.
Python json sort_keys defaults to False; raw dictionary insertion order should therefore not be mistaken for a canonical serialization policy.
Python json sort_keys=True sorts dictionary keys and is explicitly useful for stable regression comparisons.
Indentation and formatting options alter serialized JSON text, so byte-level digests require one pinned canonical serialization rather than pretty-print defaults.
FIPS 180-4 specifies secure hash algorithms used to generate message digests.
NIST states that message digests can be used to detect whether messages changed after the digest was generated.
Hash algorithm identity must be part of terminal digest provenance because FIPS 180-4 defines a family of secure hash algorithms rather than one implicit digest.
A GDAL 16-bit raster checksum is a lightweight raster QA signal, not a substitute for a byte-level secure hash because decimal floating portions are discarded.
JCS canonical serialization provides a repeatable hashable JSON representation, suitable for terminal manifest digest input.
